note: Both define a subspace as a subset closed under addition and scalar multiplication (Apostol: nonempty subset that is itself a linear space; Strang: set including 0 closed under the two operations). By Apostol's Thm 15.4 the 'itself a linear space' form is equivalent to the closure criterion, so they name the same object. s113 is phrased generally ('a subspace of a vector space'), not explicitly R^n-restricted, so strict-same rather than special-case.

Subspace closure criterion, theorem-to-theorem. Apostol Thm 15.4 (a121) is the full BICONDITIONAL: a nonempty subset is a subspace IFF it satisfies the closure axioms; its non-trivial content is the SUFFICIENCY direction (closure => the remaining axioms are inherited => subspace). Strang s104 states only the FORWARD/trivial direction: a subspace (given as such) must contain every cv+dw, folding the two closure requirements into one linear-combination condition. So s104 is a proper partial case of a121 (one direction of the iff), hence special-case with general_tok=a121, NOT strict-same. Both are theorems, so no type-flip. Confidence 0.7: the content overlap is certain, but this is a 'partial-claim' flavor of special-case (half a biconditional) rather than the R^m-instantiation flavor used elsewhere in this block. The same closure content also underlies Strang's definition s113 (matched to a101).

KEY CALL: column space vs linear span. Apostol L(S) is the set of all finite linear combinations of an arbitrary subset S (possibly infinite) of an arbitrary linear space V (possibly infinite-dimensional). Strang's column space is L(columns): the span of one specific finite set of vectors living in R^m. The construction 'set of all linear combinations, itself a subspace' is identical, but the generating set is a fixed finite family and the ambient space is R^m. It is a concrete instance of the general span, so special-case, NOT strict-same. Being strict here: strict-same would require the same generality (arbitrary/infinite S, arbitrary V), which the column space lacks.

Row space = subspace spanned by the rows = L(rows), the span of a specific finite set of vectors in R^n. Same reasoning as column space: a concrete instance of Apostol's general linear span L(S), hence special-case of a103. The 'row space' name and the C(A^T) identity are concrete matrix-specific dressing, but the mathematical object (span of a finite vector set) is an instance of L(S).

Notation-to-notation. Apostol L(S) is the general notation for the span of any set. Strang C(A) is notation for the column space = span of one matrix's columns in R^m. C(A) is the specialized/instantiated span notation, so special-case of the general L(S) notation.

Definition of 'a set spans a space': Apostol 'every element of the space is a finite linear combination of the set'; Strang 'their linear combinations fill the space'. Same spanning relation, stated generally on both sides (Strang's 'set of vectors' carries only mild R^n flavor and the definition itself is general), so strict-same. Strang's 'columns span the column space' is just an example within the same concept.

Apostol dedicates a definition object to 'finite linear combination of elements of S'. Strang's list uses linear combinations pervasively (s103, s104, s107, s113) but has no dedicated defining object for 'linear combination' in this block, so no counterpart to match.

Theorem 'every subspace contains the zero vector' (from scalar rule with c=0). Apostol has no dedicated object for this here; in Apostol it is subsumed under the linear-space axioms/closure and is not listed separately, so none.

Z, the zero vector space / zero subspace of R^3. A concrete example of a specific smallest subspace; Apostol's list has no matching object. (The zero element does appear as the span of the empty set inside a103, but s101 is the standalone concept of Z as a space, a different object.) none.

Concrete matrix notation: row space = C(A^T) and left nullspace = N(A^T), built on the transpose. Transpose, left nullspace, and the C(A^T) notation are matrix-specific with no abstract counterpart in this block. Concrete-only, none. (The row-space-as-span content overlaps s111, which is matched; s102's distinctive content is the transpose/left-nullspace notation.)

Concrete example: a plane through the origin in R^3 is a subspace; planes missing the origin are not. An illustration of the subspace concept, not a distinct definition/theorem; no dedicated Apostol counterpart. none.
Concrete example: a line through the origin in R^3 is a subspace. Illustration of the subspace concept, no dedicated Apostol counterpart. none.

Solvability theorem: Ax=b is solvable iff b lies in the column space of A. A concrete application linking linear-system solvability to the column space (span of columns). This subspace/span block of Apostol has no counterpart; concrete-only, none.
